co_mission_wall_the.blurb: A big, dark gneiss face in Clear Creek Canyon, in the Tunnel 2 West stretch, standing on the opposite bank of the creek from the Wall of the '90s. It holds fourteen routes, mainly bolted sport lines with a few trad climbs, including a well-liked 5.9+ crack. The grades lean hard: a handful of moderate routes at the bottom, a cluster in the 5.10s and 5.11s, and the bulk of the wall in the 5.12 range with one step beyond. It suits experienced sport climbers looking for steep, sustained pitches rather than beginners warming up.

co_iron_mountain.blurb: A small bouldering area near Buena Vista in the Arkansas Valley, listed within the East bouldering zone. It has fourteen problems, all boulder climbing, with a reasonably even spread from V2 up through V7 and one much harder test piece near the top of the range. Most lines sit in the V3 to V6 middle ground, so it suits climbers who already boulder comfortably and want a quieter alternative to the busier Buena Vista blocks. Bring pads and plan on a half-day visit, since the problem count is modest.

co_hobo_cave.blurb: A compact cave in a cliff band on Flagstaff Mountain above Boulder, with fourteen boulder problems. The style is steep and powerful: roof moves, long traverses along the cave walls, and a slab on the right side, with many problems being links or variations of one another. Grades run from easy up to V9, with most of the problems in the V4 to V8 band, so it favors strong boulderers over beginners. The overhang usually keeps the cave dry and climbable in a wide range of weather, which makes it a handy fallback on damp days.

co_deer_ridge_buttress.blurb: A tall granite cliff of roughly 600 feet on Deer Mountain's north side in Rocky Mountain National Park, above Estes Park. Climbing here is mostly multi-pitch trad, with one aid line, and the routes are long, committing days. Difficulty runs from easy fourth-class terrain through a good number of 5.8 and 5.9 lines, with the largest group at 5.10 and a single 5.11. It is high, quiet and often solitary, and the approach is a real effort, so it suits parties comfortable with alpine-style trad and a long uphill walk.

co_boxcar_the.blurb: A large sandstone boulder beside the trail to X Rock, just north of Durango. All fourteen problems are bouldering, spread from very easy to V7 with the largest cluster at V3, plus a few harder ones in the V5 to V7 range. That makes it friendly to mixed groups, since newer boulderers have several warm-ups while stronger climbers have a handful of tougher lines. It is a short stop right next to the crag's approach trail, handy for a quick session before or after roped climbing at X Rock.

co_5_iron_side_wall.blurb: A granite sport wall on Monitor Rock, in the Independence Pass area near Aspen. The wall sits just up the trail from Boulder Wall, left of Trailhead Wall, and is a short walk from the road. Its single-pitch bolted routes range from about 40 to 125 feet. Two easy lines near the left end serve beginners, but most of the fourteen routes are 5.11, with a few at 5.10 and 5.12, so it is mainly a wall for intermediate to advanced sport climbers who want steady, short-approach climbing at altitude.

co_scorpio_dome.blurb: A secluded south-facing granite dome in Pike National Forest, reached from Rampart Range Road between Denver and Colorado Springs. It is mostly a trad crag, with cracks from fingers to hands and wider, plus slab and a few sport lines, top-rope problems and boulders. Of the fourteen climbs, routes sit at 5.8, 5.10 and 5.11, with the 5.10 crack tier the main draw. The sun hits most of the day, and the crowds are thin compared with busier Front Range crags, so it rewards climbers who are comfortable placing gear and finding their own way in.
